title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging
authors: Sami Alnawali, Muhammad Atif Saeed, Abdul Hadi, Azka Atiq, Akhtar Jamil, Ahmad Din
abstract: Deep learning shows promise for breast cancer diagnosis, but limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption. We benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained models (ResNet50, VGG19, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, Xception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, and Swin Transformer) for benign-versus-malignant classification on the BreakHis histopathology dataset using a patient-level split, and explain their predictions with Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP. DenseNet121 performed best, with 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999, and significantly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001). Transformer-based models trailed the CNNs. The explanations consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance. Combining transfer learning with explainable AI can thus yield accurate, interpretable tools for breast cancer diagnosis.

infographic.key_insight: DenseNet121 led ten pretrained models in classifying benign versus malignant breast histopathology images, achieving 99.4% test accuracy and 0.999 AUC-ROC.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Explainable image classification may support breast pathology research, but these results do not establish readiness for clinical diagnosis.
method: Benchmarked ten ImageNet-pretrained CNN and transformer models on BreakHis histopathology images.
Used a patient-level split for benign-versus-malignant classification.
Applied Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP; explanations highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the BreakHis patient-level test split, DenseNet121 reportedly outperformed all other models significantly (p < 0.001), while transformers trailed CNNs.
infographic.watch_item: External validation and prospective clinical evaluation are not reported in the abstract, limiting conclusions about real-world generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging

title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents
authors: Sirry Chen, Fangke Chen, Xuanwen Ding, Wei Chen, Zhongyu Wei
abstract: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.

infographic.key_insight: ClinVerse moves medical AI training and evaluation beyond static questions into interactive diagnostic scenarios with feedback on the full decision-making process.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The environment tests how agents gather patient information, request examinations, and reach diagnoses, but does not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Grounds simulated interactions in ClinPatient, a dataset of 150,000 diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records.
Coordinates six specialized clinical roles as a doctor agent interviews patients, requests examinations, and produces a diagnosis.
Uses rule-based trajectory scores for information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy to support training and evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluations of general-purpose and medical-domain models, with nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improving diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse.
infographic.watch_item: Improvements within a scored simulation may not translate to safe, effective care; the abstract reports no prospective clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents

title: Radiology Guideline-derived Decision Graph for Efficient Clinical Decision Support
authors: Xuewen Zhou, Zhen Chen
abstract: Radiological risk stratification and management planning are essential downstream tasks in medical imaging. Automating these tasks is challenging because clinical guideline criteria are distributed across prose, tables, and cross-referenced definitions. We present Guideline-derived Decision Graph (GDGraph), a framework that decouples guideline compilation from case evaluation. During compilation, a large language model partitions guidelines into section-based chunks, extracts local decision subgraphs with linked definitions, and aggregates related branches into an executable decision graph. During inference, a fast System One model answers localized clinical questions while deterministic traversal resolves Boolean logic, turning opaque single-pass predictions into a traceable decision path without task-specific training. Across 347 cases spanning renal cyst, adnexal mass, and thyroid nodule guidelines, GDGraph improves System One accuracy from 57.3% to 90.8%, outperforming retrieval-augmented GPT-4o (80.1%) and graph-guided GPT-4o with chain-of-thought (82.7%) at substantially lower latency and cost. The source code will be available.

infographic.key_insight: GDGraph converts radiology guidelines into executable decision graphs, improving case-evaluation accuracy while making decision paths traceable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more consistent guideline-based risk stratification and management planning for renal cysts, adnexal masses, and thyroid nodules.
method: An LLM partitions guidelines into sections and extracts decision subgraphs with linked definitions.
Related branches are compiled into an executable decision graph.
A fast model answers localized clinical questions while deterministic traversal resolves Boolean logic.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 347 cases, GDGraph improved System One accuracy from 57.3% to 90.8%, exceeding retrieval-augmented GPT-4o (80.1%) and graph-guided GPT-4o with chain-of-thought (82.7%), with lower reported latency and cost.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical performance; guideline-compilation accuracy and generalizability require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Radiology Guideline-derived Decision Graph for Efficient Clinical Decision Support

title: Quantifying Localized Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes by Deep Learning on H&E Images: Analytical Validation and Prognostic Value in Lung Adenocarcinoma
authors: Osinski, B. L.; Ingale, K.; Huang, A.; Terdich, B.; Muller, Y.; Joshi, R. P.; Miotto, R.; Jones, R. D.; Beaubier, N.; Sangli, C.
abstract: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are a critical determinant of response to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). However, assessing the clinical utility of TIL quantification is challenging due to subjective manual scoring and differences in methodology, including some that may obscure localized immune responses critical to ICI response. Together, these issues limit our understanding of potential prognostic benefits of performing routine TIL quantification. Here, we present the "focal TIL score," an artificial intelligence-powered biomarker derived from routinely generated Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) pathology images which measures TIL density within tiles across the entire relevant tissue region in order to account for spatial heterogeneity of localized lymphocytic infiltration. Underlying this method are two deep learning models that ensure accurate, reproducible, and interpretable quantification: one for lymphocyte detection trained on IHC-derived ground truth, and one for segmentation of tumor and tumor-adjacent stroma region ("scorable region") trained on consensus pathologist annotations. We performed an analytical validation of the two models, demonstrating high overall performance: lymphocyte model concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) = 0.90, scorable region model Dice score = 0.87. We then performed a prognostic association study in a cohort of 685 ICI-treated LUAD patients and saw that, the focal TIL score was significantly associated with overall survival (HR=0.60, 95% CI 0.48-0.75, P<0.001), outperforming the standard biomarker PD-L1. Our findings show that quantifying the spatial intensity of immune infiltration, rather than the global average, provides a superior measure of the anti-tumor immune response. The accessibility and standardization associated with this approach may enable further studies and developments in precision oncology for LUAD.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-derived focal TIL score captures localized immune infiltration on routine H&E images and was associated with overall survival in ICI-treated lung adenocarcinoma.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The score may support prognostic research using routine pathology slides, but the reported association does not establish its ability to predict benefit from immunotherapy.
method: Detect lymphocytes with a deep learning model trained on IHC-derived ground truth.
Segment tumor and adjacent stroma using a model trained on consensus pathologist annotations.
Measure tile-level lymphocyte density to capture spatially localized infiltration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical validation yielded lymphocyte CCC 0.90 and segmentation Dice 0.87; in 685 ICI-treated patients, the score was associated with overall survival (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.48–0.75; P<0.001) and reportedly outperformed PD-L1.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability across laboratories and prospective clinical utility require further validation before routine use.
infographic.paper_title: Quantifying Localized Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes by Deep Learning on H&E Images: Analytical Validation and Prognostic Value in Lung Adenocarcinoma

title: A 211K Parameter Foundation Model: Genetic Prompting in Neural Cellular Automata
authors: John Kalkhof, Niklas Ihm, Daniel Kirste, Anirban Mukhopadhyay
abstract: The scale of modern foundation models enables broad task generalization. In medical imaging, where segmentation demands vary widely across clinical contexts, such flexibility is invaluable. But current models, such as SAM trade adaptability for scale, locking their utility behind high-end infrastructure and leaving behind the low-resource environments most in need of diagnostic support. To bridge this gap, we introduce Foundational-NCA, a lightweight foundation model capable of adapting to a wide range of medical segmentation tasks without retraining. Built on Neural Cellular Automata (NCA), Foundational-NCA incorporates gradient-based learning with genetic optimization over a latent task space, using a compact task vector to guide predictions. This enables dynamic adaptation via a genetic prompt mechanism, allowing the model to generalize across tasks while keeping the parameter count magnitudes lower at just 211 thousand, compared to SAM-based models with 38.9 to 636 million parameters. We evaluate Foundational-NCA on 15 trained and 6 entirely unseen segmentation tasks from the TotalSegmentator dataset, achieving an average Dice score of 84.5% on known tasks and 60.4% on unseen ones. These results demonstrate that task generalization is possible in ultra-compact models, laying the groundwork for resource-efficient, deployable foundation models in clinical environments where infrastructure is limited. By reducing model size by over 180 times, Foundational-NCA takes a step toward a more equitable future for medical AI, one where powerful tools are within reach of every healthcare setting.

infographic.key_insight: Foundational-NCA uses just 211,000 parameters to adapt to medical image segmentation tasks through genetic prompting without retraining.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Its compact size could support segmentation tools in resource-limited healthcare settings, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Builds on Neural Cellular Automata.
Combines gradient-based learning with genetic optimization in a latent task space.
Uses a compact task vector to guide segmentation predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On TotalSegmentator, evaluation covered 15 trained and 6 unseen segmentation tasks, with average Dice scores of 84.5% and 60.4%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Lower performance on unseen tasks warrants further validation before deployment, and parameter count alone does not establish runtime efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: A 211K Parameter Foundation Model: Genetic Prompting in Neural Cellular Automata

title: Large Language Models for Accurate Medical Chart Abstraction: Enabling Scalable and Secure Artificial Intelligence Deployment in Stroke
authors: Zhusi Zhong, Carl M. Porto, David Hong, Miranda Gonzales, Revyn Kim, Gnaneswari Karayi
abstract: Medical chart abstraction transforms unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring. We evaluated a prompting-based large language model (LLM) framework for extracting eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals. Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs were evaluated across architectures, model sizes, and biomedical adaptations using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard. Evaluation was restricted to report-variable pairs with a valid LLaMA3.3-70B CoT prediction and a corresponding reference label. Performance measures included extraction accuracy, inference latency, and agreement with expert adjudication. Twenty discordant cases per variable underwent review by two senior physicians and four medical students. LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved performance on inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication showed that AI predictions were more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge. Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.

infographic.key_insight: LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall chart-abstraction accuracy at 94.8%, with prompting benefits varying by clinical variable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Locally deployed LLMs could help scale retrospective stroke registry curation and quality monitoring, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.
method: Extracted eight clinical variables from 2,416 acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals.
Compared 22 instruction-tuned open-source LLMs using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Measured accuracy and latency against non-expert annotations, with expert review of selected discordant cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation included only report-variable pairs with valid LLaMA3.3-70B Chain-of-Thought predictions and reference labels; two senior physicians and four medical students reviewed 20 discordant cases per variable.
infographic.watch_item: Prediction-based inclusion and selective expert review limit interpretation of overall performance; intracranial angioplasty extraction remained challenging.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Models for Accurate Medical Chart Abstraction: Enabling Scalable and Secure Artificial Intelligence Deployment in Stroke

title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical Decision Support
authors: Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Moon-Il Joo, Hee-Cheol Kim
abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.

infographic.key_insight: DocTalk’s chart-grounded instruction tuning improved medical question-answering performance across six open-source language models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could help clinicians retrieve information from discharge summaries, but improved benchmark performance does not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
method: Generated 500 QA pairs from de-identified discharge summaries using sentence decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review.
Evaluated three general-purpose and three biomedical models before and after LoRA instruction tuning.
Tested the two top-performing models on PubMedQA to assess external generalization.

title: TRACER, a time-to-event EHR foundation model for disease detection across health systems
authors: Mara Pleasure, Ekaterina Redekop, Vedrana Ivezic, Rushikesh Kulkarni, Aaron Chin, William Speier
abstract: Foundation models trained on longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can predict clinical diagnoses years in the future, making them a potential tool for disease screening. We developed TRACER (Temporal Risk Assessment with Clinical EHR Representations), a decoder-based foundation model pretrained on data from over 4.5 million patients from four health systems, and evaluated it on 16 incident diseases at 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons in more than 2 million patients from two health systems excluded from model development. In contrast to typical evaluations that focus on global metrics (e.g., AUROC), we measured performance at the low false-positive rates that are realistic for screening. We found that TRACER retained its discrimination in external health systems, and at 95% specificity, the patients it flagged were up to eight times more likely to be diagnosed within a year than unselected patients. Evaluating at this operating point also revealed what global metrics alone did not: detection and false-alert burden varied across diseases and health systems, even when discrimination appeared stable. Our results illustrate the potential of foundation models for screening and underscore the need for evaluation in health systems excluded from development to assess disease detection and false-alert burden at levels appropriate for intended clinical use.}

infographic.key_insight: TRACER predicted future diagnoses across external health systems, with flagged patients up to eight times more likely to receive a diagnosis within one year at 95% specificity.
infographic.clinical_relevance: EHR-based risk prediction could help target disease screening, but detection and false-alert burden vary by disease and health system.
method: Decoder-based foundation model pretrained on longitudinal EHRs from over 4.5 million patients across four health systems.
Evaluated 16 incident diseases at 1-, 2-, and 5-year prediction horizons.
Assessed screening performance at low false-positive rates, including 95% specificity.
infographic.evidence_signal: External evaluation included more than 2 million patients from two health systems excluded from model development, where discrimination was retained.
infographic.watch_item: Stable overall discrimination did not ensure consistent detection or false-alert burden; local validation is needed before screening implementation.
infographic.paper_title: TRACER, a time-to-event EHR foundation model for disease detection across health systems

title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
authors: Simon A. Lee, Jiahang Sha, Moonseong Jeong, Yunbei Pan, Jeffrey N. Chiang
abstract: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approaching published GPT 4 performance while maintaining well calibrated confidence estimates (ECE 0.028 to 0.063). On patient level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In Hospital Mortality, exceeding XGBoost (0.902), but underperforms supervised models on operational outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Patient level predictions also exhibit substantial miscalibration (In Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). We introduce a lightweight, two parameter recalibration method that adapts predictions to local patient populations using 50 to 200 labeled examples, reducing ECE to 0.007. Our findings establish open System One models as a promising zero shot baseline for medical AI, combining competitive predictive performance with low computational cost and efficient local calibration. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.

infographic.key_insight: MedJev delivers competitive zero-shot medical predictions in a single forward pass on a laptop, but patient-level confidence estimates need local recalibration.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Low computational demands could support locally run clinical decision-support research, though predictive performance alone does not establish clinical safety or benefit.
method: Evaluated an open System One model across 10 medical benchmarks.
Compared zero-shot predictions with LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models.
Tested two-parameter local recalibration using 50–200 labeled examples.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MIMIC-IV patient-level tasks, mortality AUROC was 0.926 versus XGBoost’s 0.902, while ED admission AUROC was lower than a supervised comparator (0.745 versus 0.809); recalibration reduced reported ECE from 0.286 to 0.007.
infographic.watch_item: Strong discrimination did not ensure reliable confidence estimates, and performance varied by task; local validation and calibration remain important before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine

title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
authors: Roxana Ramona Szomiu, George Ursu, Adrian Groza
abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.

infographic.key_insight: The proposed framework combines ontology grounding with multi-agent reasoning to make differential diagnosis more explicit, traceable, and evidence-linked.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It aims to support reviewable diagnostic reasoning and targeted follow-up questions when patient descriptions are incomplete or ambiguous.
method: Ground diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base.
Decompose differential diagnosis into explicit, auditable multi-agent reasoning steps.
Identify discriminative missing symptoms and generate targeted follow-up questions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports publicly available source code but provides no dataset details, evaluation metrics, or quantitative results supporting its claimed improvements.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability may depend on ontology coverage and quality; clinical performance remains unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities evolve across a longitudinal care pathway. Here we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from longitudinal records of 405 patients across two cancer centers, the benchmark comprises 941 patient-phase units across six sequential care phases and 17,688 patient-specific atomic criteria spanning five evaluation dimensions, with each assessment strictly restricted to decision-time clinical evidence. Evaluating 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs revealed that strong diagnostic performance does not carry over to downstream care. We evaluated 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, showing that high diagnostic performance did not translate into improved downstream care. Instead, the dominant failure modes reversed across phases. Explicit decision errors dominated anatomical staging at 48.2%, whereas decision omissions dominated initial work-up and post-treatment follow-up at 33.4% and 30.4%, respectively. In the evaluated model set, medically adapted models showed higher omission rates than general-purpose models. Moreover, varying query granularity exposes a critical specification trade-off: broad open-ended requests degrade Decision Quality across all 30 models, while more detailed, checklist-like prompts raise Decision Quality but reduce Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence. Furthermore, NPC-RubricBench demonstrates that static diagnostic benchmarks are insufficient to ensure consistent clinical reliability over time, highlighting the importance of phase-adaptive safeguards in multistage medical AI.

infographic.key_insight: Strong diagnostic performance did not ensure reliable downstream cancer care, with dominant LLM failure modes shifting across care phases.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings support phase-specific evaluation and safeguards rather than relying on diagnostic accuracy alone to assess clinical reliability.
method: Developed NPC-RubricBench from longitudinal nasopharyngeal carcinoma records across six care phases.
Scored 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs using patient-specific criteria restricted to decision-time evidence.
Compared failure patterns across phases and tested broad versus checklist-like prompts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark included 405 patients from two cancer centers, 941 patient-phase units, and 17,688 atomic criteria across five evaluation dimensions.
infographic.watch_item: More detailed prompts improved Decision Quality but reduced Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence, highlighting a trade-off in prompt design.
infographic.paper_title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care

title: Simulating Psychotherapeutic Sessions with Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Proof-of-Concept Study of In Silico Psychotherapy Research
authors: Horvath, K.; Longani, S.; Brill, S.; Ballantyne, H. A.; Schaefert, R.; Tegethoff, M.; Schirmer, L.; Boerner, E.; Timm, I. J.; Elyoseph, Z.; Meinlschmidt, G. P.
abstract: BackgroundAcross biomedicine, in silico models increasingly complement in vivo and in vitro research. Psychotherapy science, however, remains constrained by methodological limitations, resource-intensive trials, challenges in manipulating clinically meaningful features experimentally, and a potential ceiling in efficacy. Leveraging generative AI and large language models (LLMs), we propose a framework for "in silico psychotherapy research": controlled simulations of psychotherapeutic interactions under reproducible experimental conditions. ObjectiveWe test whether such simulation experiments can recover a theoretically expected effect of an isolated psychotherapy-process manipulation. MethodsIn a preregistered proof-of-concept study, we generated 512 fully automated motivational interviewing (MI) sessions by linking locally deployed Llama-3.3-70B-In-struct based therapist and patient models across eight vignettes and eight therapist personas. Therapist, but not patient, prompts manipulated common therapeutic factors (CTF), contrasting high versus low empathy, affirmation, and alliance building behaviour in a controlled design. The primary outcome was MI treatment integrity (MITI 4.2 global ratings), assessed by a blinded LLM with repeated ratings and analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Secondary outcomes included observer-inferred importance/confidence rulers based on simulated patient utterances; Therapist Empathy Scale (TES) and Working Alliance Inventory-Short Observer (WAI-S-O) served as manipulation fidelity checks. Human coders rated a stratified subsample. ResultsOf the 512 simulations, 506 (98.8%) yielded complete transcripts and 480 (93.75) were retained for analysis. Manipulation checks confirmed the fidelity of the CTF manipulation (WAI-S-O total scores {beta}=3.14; [2.65,3.63], p<0.001, TES {beta}=14.48 [13.92,15.04], p<0.001). High versus low CTF produced a theoretically expected improvement in all MITI global ratings, including the MI-specific features not directly targeted by the CTF manipulation ({beta}=0.54-0.95; all p<0.001). Simulated patient confidence but not importance for change increased more under high CTF ({beta}=0.17 [0.09,0.26], p<0.001). Human ratings confirmed the direction of the primary contrast. ConclusionsLLM-based psychotherapy simulations were technically feasible, demonstrated experimental fidelity, and showed theoretically concordant effects beyond directly manipulated constructs and simulation participants. These findings provide proof of concept for in silico psychotherapy research as a promising complementary pre-clinical experimental paradigm for hypothesis generation and testing to support accelerated intervention development. The applicability of this approach across patient populations, therapeutic modalities and model architectures requires further evaluation. Trial Pre-registrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT06813066; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06813066?term=NCT06813066

infographic.key_insight: AI-simulated psychotherapy sessions reproduced the expected link between stronger empathy, affirmation, and alliance building and higher motivational interviewing quality ratings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Controlled simulations could complement psychotherapy research, but these findings do not establish benefits for real patients.

Manipulated therapist prompts to produce high versus low levels of common therapeutic factors.
Evaluated sessions using blinded, repeated LLM ratings and mixed-effects models; human coders rated a stratified subsample.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 512 simulations, 480 were analyzed; high-factor sessions scored higher on all motivational interviewing global ratings (β=0.54–0.95; all p<0.001).
infographic.watch_item: LLM-generated interactions and primarily LLM-based ratings may share biases; simulated improvements require validation against human therapy data.
infographic.paper_title: Simulating Psychotherapeutic Sessions with Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Proof-of-Concept Study of In Silico Psychotherapy Research

title: Segment Anything Model Based Context Guided Mamba Unet for Medical Image Segmentation
authors: Chenchen Wang, You Zhou
abstract: Medical image segmentation is crucial for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning, requiring both global contextual understanding and fine-grained structural precision. While the Segment Anything Model (SAM) demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, its direct application to medical images often lacks domain-specific adaptability. Meanwhile, State Space Models (SSMs)-based methods, such as Mamba, efficiently capture long-range dependencies but may struggle with preserving fine anatomical details. To address these challenges, we propose a segment anything model based context guided mamba unet, SAMBA-UNet, a novel framework that integrates SAM's context knowledge with Mamba's hierarchical feature learning to enhance both global representation and local detail refinement. Specifically, we introduce the Hierarchical Context Enhancement Module (HCEM), an attention-based fusion module that deeply incorporates the multi-level features of SAM and Mamba to improve detail perception and segmentation precision. Additionally, we employ LoRA and Adapter-based fine-tuning to adapt SAM to medical imaging tasks, further enhancing its domain-specific segmentation capability and robustness. We conducted a comprehensive study on several medical segmentation datasets, including Synapse, ISIC17, and ISIC18, evaluating our method across multiple metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMBA-UNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively balancing generalization, segmentation accuracy, and computational efficiency. Our code will be released upon acceptance.

infographic.key_insight: SAMBA-UNet combines SAM’s contextual features with Mamba’s hierarchical learning to improve global understanding and fine-detail segmentation in medical images.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More precise segmentation could support diagnosis and treatment planning, but the abstract does not establish clinical benefit or readiness for deployment.
method: Integrates SAM and Mamba within a U-Net framework.
Uses a Hierarchical Context Enhancement Module for attention-based, multilevel feature fusion.
Adapts SAM to medical images using LoRA and Adapter-based fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on Synapse, ISIC17, and ISIC18 reportedly achieved state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics, though the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Computational efficiency and robustness claims need verification from detailed results and external validation before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Segment Anything Model Based Context Guided Mamba Unet for Medical Image Segmentation

title: Fu-TCM: a multimodal large language model that learns traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic reasoning
authors: Jiahang Xie, Tong Jin, Lingfei Wu, Yaping You, Jie Huang, Yuanchang Jin
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Fu-TCM-27B led six TCM benchmarks, suggesting that structured reasoning supervision can improve automated syndrome differentiation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model may support research into TCM diagnostic reasoning, but these benchmark results do not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
method: Trained on cleaned and filtered data from an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples.
Combined classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and public datasets.
Used Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization to reward response format, intermediate reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six TCM reasoning, text and vision benchmarks, Fu-TCM-27B achieved 81.01% macro-average accuracy, exceeding the strongest reference model with complete results by 7.13 percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports benchmark evaluation, not prospective clinical validation; real-world reliability remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Fu-TCM: a multimodal large language model that learns traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic reasoning

title: Responsible Quantum Machine Learning for Medical Imaging: A Fairness Audit Across Sensitive Subgroups
authors: Giovanni dos Santos Franco, Felipe Mahlow, Ellison Fernando Cardoso, José Adenaldo Santos Bittencourt, Felipe Fanchini
abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) is increasingly explored for medical classification, yet its behaviour under subgroup-aware fairness criteria remains understudied. We present an empirical fairness audit of classical and quantum classifiers for medical imaging, assuming QML is not inherently fair. Two scenarios are evaluated: dermatological lesions on DDI (sensitive attribute: Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays on CheXpert-derived data (sensitive attribute: age group). Using ResNet-18 embeddings, we train SVM, MLP, QSVM and QCNN under a baseline and three mitigation settings: differentiable Equalized Odds (EO) regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning (GRL), and both combined. Foundation models (PanDerm, EVA-X) serve as external references. Quantum classifiers may achieve competitive aggregate performance while still exhibiting subgroup disparities. Since a smaller subgroup AUC gap may stem from degrading the best group rather than improving the worst, each mitigation is also tested against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin relative to its baseline. Under this criterion, several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, are not clinically acceptable due to loss of global discrimination. On DDI, QSVM with GRL+EO performed best and approached PanDerm in the performance/fairness trade-off; on CheXpert, QCNN with GRL achieved the highest aggregate performance but increased disparity, and EVA-X remained stronger. Fairness effects are model- and dataset-dependent, so QML requires empirical subgroup-aware evaluation. All quantum models run in classical simulation; we claim no quantum advantage.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum classifiers can achieve competitive overall performance while retaining subgroup disparities, and smaller fairness gaps can mask performance losses.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Medical imaging AI should be evaluated for both subgroup disparities and preserved overall discrimination before clinical use is considered.
method: Compared SVM, MLP, QSVM and QCNN using ResNet-18 image embeddings.
Tested Equalized Odds regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning and their combination against baseline models.
Assessed subgroup AUC gaps and a pre-specified non-inferiority margin, with PanDerm and EVA-X as external references.
infographic.evidence_signal: Audits covered DDI skin lesions by Fitzpatrick skin type and CheXpert-derived chest X-rays by age group, finding model- and dataset-dependent fairness effects.
infographic.watch_item: All quantum models ran in classical simulation; the study claims no quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Responsible Quantum Machine Learning for Medical Imaging: A Fairness Audit Across Sensitive Subgroups

title: Enhancing Atrial Fibrillation Detection Through Hyperparameter Optimization
authors: Sara Gjorgjieva, Ilinka Ivanoska, Marjan Gusev
abstract: This study explores the role of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) in enhancing the detection of Atrial Fibrillation (AF) using both machine learning and deep learning models. We evaluated a range of standard classifiers - Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost classifiers, alongside deep learning architectures including Recurrent Neural Networks, Deep Neural Networks, and Siamese Neural Networks. To fine-tune these models, we applied four HPO methods: Genetic Algorithm, Hyperband, Optuna, and SMAC3. The experiments were conducted using inter-patient and intra- patient data splits to assess model generalization and robustness in the presence of class imbalance, which is reflective of real-world AF occurrence. Our results, based on PhysioNet electrocardiogram datasets, showed that the Hyperband-optimized XGBoost model outperformed all others, achieving a peak F1 score of 96.95%. These findings highlight the critical role of suitable HPO strategies in enhancing the accuracy and robustness of AF classification outcomes in clinical settings.

infographic.key_insight: Hyperband-optimized XGBoost achieved the highest reported AF detection performance, with a peak F1 score of 96.95%.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Optimizing ECG-based AF detection models may support more reliable screening, but this study does not establish clinical readiness.
method: Compared Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost classifiers with recurrent, deep, and Siamese neural networks.
Tuned models using Genetic Algorithm, Hyperband, Optuna, and SMAC3.
Evaluated inter-patient and intra-patient splits under class imbalance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments used PhysioNet ECG datasets with inter-patient and intra-patient evaluation; the abstract does not specify which split yielded the peak F1 score.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report external clinical validation, so generalization to new patient populations remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Enhancing Atrial Fibrillation Detection Through Hyperparameter Optimization

title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
authors: Samuel Schmidgall, Tim Strother, Alex Bijamov, Min Woo Sun, Anil Palepu, Akshay Goel
abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

infographic.key_insight: Simulation-based reinforcement learning improved a language model’s psychiatric intake performance, outperforming its identically prompted base model in 76.7% of matched scenarios.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings suggest potential to support structured psychiatric intake, but do not establish safety or effectiveness in real-world patient care.
method: Trained a language model through multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulated psychiatric intake encounters.
Compared trained and base models in a randomized, double-blind crossover study with psychiatrist-enacted patients and independent psychiatrist raters.
Stress-tested conversational safety using 256 adversarial presentations derived from Delphi-consensus taxonomies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 60 matched scenario pairs (120 encounters), the trained model improved clinical rubric scores (d_z = 0.77); adversarial testing found lower acute-risk under-triage (12.9% vs. 30.5%).
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation used simulated and psychiatrist-enacted encounters; residual safety gaps require safeguards, clinician oversight, and real-world validation.
infographic.paper_title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake

title: InfantNet: A Large Scale Dataset for Infant Body Pose and Shape Estimation
authors: Zhipeng Hui, Jiahao Wang, Xun Dong, Guofeng Zhang, Xingrui Wang, Jiawei Peng
abstract: Infant pose and shape estimation is essential for applications in childcare, developmental monitoring, and medical diagnosis. However, existing methods and datasets are largely designed for adults, and direct transfer to infants fails due to substantial differences in body proportions, articulation limits, and frequent self-occlusion. To address this gap, we introduce InfantNet, the largest real-image infant dataset to date, comprising 108,902 RGB images of infants aged 6-18 months. Each image is annotated with 2D keypoints, and a curated subset of 11,642 images additionally includes 3D pose and shape annotations with full SMIL parameters, verified through multi-view rendering and reprojection-error filtering. We use an iterative annotation pipeline to ensure high fidelity across both 2D and 3D labels. InfantNet establishes a large-scale, comprehensive benchmark for infant 2D keypoint detection and 3D pose-and-shape recovery. Baseline experiments demonstrate that state-of-the-art adult pose estimators do not generalize well to infants, whereas fine-tuning on InfantNet yields a consistent improvement. The gains are even more pronounced for 3D pose and shape estimation, where SMIL-based estimation demonstrates robust performance with accuracy comparable to results reported for SMPL-based models. By releasing the InfantNet dataset and benchmark, we provide a vital resource for advancing infant pose analysis and related healthcare applications.

infographic.key_insight: InfantNet provides a large infant-specific benchmark that improves pose and body-shape estimation over direct transfer of adult-trained models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The dataset could support research in developmental monitoring and infant movement analysis, but clinical utility is not established in the abstract.
method: Collect 108,902 RGB images of infants aged 6–18 months and annotate 2D keypoints.
Add 3D pose and shape labels with full SMIL parameters for 11,642 images.
Use iterative annotation, multi-view rendering, and reprojection-error filtering to refine labels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmark experiments report consistent gains after infant-specific fine-tuning, especially for 3D estimation, but the abstract provides no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Performance outside the 6–18-month age range and in clinical settings remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: InfantNet: A Large Scale Dataset for Infant Body Pose and Shape Estimation

title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Anna Kadi, Natali Borrego, Sukru Aras, Michael L. Ferm
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.

infographic.key_insight: CEDAR, an evidence-citing and self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine-learning models in predicting pediatric diabetes outcomes, with the largest gains on sparsely screened outcomes.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings suggest potential for chart-grounded risk prediction in youth with diabetes, but do not establish improved care or readiness for clinical use.
method: Used 18 months of multimodal records to predict outcomes at 24 months.
Combined structured data and note-derived social determinants, plus continuous glucose monitoring data for type 1 diabetes.
Predicted seven type 2 diabetes outcomes and four shared outcomes in type 1 diabetes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 2,489 youth with type 2 and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes, pooled AUROC was 0.815 and 0.756, respectively, versus 0.656–0.700 and 0.603–0.631 for trained machine-learning comparators.
infographic.watch_item: External and prospective validation are not described in the abstract, leaving generalizability and real-world clinical benefit uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records

title: Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: temporal extraction of comorbidities from unstructured clinical text using a large language model
authors: Filchenko, I.; Dennstaedt, F.; Zub, K.; Pompizii, F. I.; van der Meer, J.; Adamantidis, A.; Cihoric, N.; Schmidt, M. H.; Bassetti, C. L.
abstract: IntroductionLarge language models (LLMs) may enable the extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured electronic health records, but most previous work focused on identifying diagnoses without preserving their temporal context. We evaluated the ability of an LLM to extract diagnoses and associated dates from longitudinal clinical reports. MethodsIn an observational study using the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry, diagnostic annotations from 248 patients comprising 2343 clinical entries were analyzed. Six common comorbidity groups, subdivided into 32 hierarchical diagnostic categories, were evaluated. Using gpt-oss-20b, we extracted diagnosis presence, the number of diagnostic instances, and dates per instance. A reference standard was established through independent review by two physicians, with disagreements adjudicated by a third physician. LLM performance was assessed using diagnostic classification and temporal agreement. Direct annotation costs were compared. ResultsAt the patient level, the LLM achieved an overall F1 score of 0.88 for diagnosis presence and 0.96 for the presence of a reported date. For the earliest reported diagnosis date, agreement with the reference standard was 86.73% at the day level. When considering the cumulative set of dates for each diagnosis, date recall was 87.63%, the extra-date rate was 20.88%, and full agreement was achieved in 58.19% of cases. Human annotators showed substantial disagreement in temporal annotation, with a date recall of 75.49%, an extra-date rate of 17.89%, and full agreement in 58.64% of cases. LLM-based extraction reduced direct annotation costs by 94.65%. ConclusionsLLMs can extract diagnoses and their dates from heterogeneous clinical text with high agreement with an adjudicated reference standard. These findings support the scalable use of LLMs for longitudinal clinical registries.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM extracted comorbidities and their dates from clinical text with high agreement for diagnosis presence and earliest reported dates, but lower agreement for complete date sets.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated temporal extraction could support longitudinal registry development while reducing direct annotation costs.
method: Applied gpt-oss-20b to 2,343 clinical entries from 248 Bern Sleep-Wake Registry patients.
Extracted diagnosis presence, instance counts, and dates across 32 diagnostic categories in six comorbidity groups.
Compared outputs with an adjudicated physician reference standard and assessed direct annotation costs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Diagnosis-presence F1 was 0.88, earliest-date day-level agreement was 86.73%, and direct annotation costs were reduced by 94.65%.
infographic.watch_item: Complete date-set agreement was only 58.19%, with a 20.88% extra-date rate; temporal outputs need careful validation before downstream use.
infographic.paper_title: Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: temporal extraction of comorbidities from unstructured clinical text using a large language model
